```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 120)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
```

This package helps analysts understand how well their data can support a
predictive model, with a specific focus on the out-of-sample $R^2$ and the
out-of-sample correlation $r$ that can be expected. The calculations require
no outcome data.

```{r setup}
library(predpower)
```

## What the design tells you without an outcome

Four design parameters determine expected out-of-sample accuracy: the sample
size `n`, the number of predictors `p`, the in-sample signal `rho2_in`, and a
design efficiency factor. Only the third involves an outcome, and at the
planning stage it is assumed rather than measured — exactly as an effect size
is in a power analysis.

The design efficiency factor `Dstar` ($D^*$) summarizes how leverage is
spread across the rows of the predictor matrix $X$. It is the ratio of the
prediction penalty an evenly balanced design would incur to the penalty this
design actually incurs: 1 when leverage is spread evenly across observations,
falling toward 0 as it concentrates on a few.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rlnorm(200 * 5), 200, 5)   # five skewed covariates
de <- design_efficiency(X)
de
```

In this example, five highly skewed covariates reduce the design's predictive
efficiency to `r round(100 * de$Dstar)`% of what an evenly balanced design of
the same size would deliver — a loss of about
`r round(100 * (1 - de$Dstar))`%.

Least squares and ridge regression have different efficiency factors. Ridge
leverage, at the penalty $\kappa^*$ the design implies, is flatter than
least-squares leverage, so the ridge factor $D^*(\kappa^*)$ is typically
higher than $D^*$. With a covariate matrix in hand, the package computes both.
Without one, you must state both; using $D^*$ for both is conservative for
ridge.

## A worked example

The `phonestudy` data are design summaries from a published study that
predicted personality from passively logged smartphone behavior
(Stachl et al. 2020), following the analysis of Pargent et al. (2023): 620
participants, 1,821 behavioral features aggregated over several weeks
(missing values replaced by each feature's median), and the sociability facet
of Extraversion as the outcome. Here we focus on nested predictor sets of the
first $p$ = 25, 100 and 600 features of one random ordering, and on the full
set of 1,821.

```{r}
ds <- phonestudy$designs
raw <- ds[ds$scale == "raw", ]
raw[, c("p", "n", "Dstar", "max_leverage", "Dstar_ridge", "p_eff")]
```

For the three designs that least squares can fit, `Dstar` runs from
`r f3(min(raw$Dstar, na.rm = TRUE))` to `r f3(max(raw$Dstar, na.rm = TRUE))`:
these designs deliver between about a sixth and seven-tenths of what an
evenly balanced design of the same size would. With all 1,821 features,
$p + 1 > n$ and least squares is undefined, so `Dstar` is `NA`. The ridge
factor `Dstar_ridge` is close to 1 throughout. (`Dstar_ridge` and `p_eff`
depend on `rho2_in` through $\kappa^*$; the data report them at each design's
ridge break-even, defined below.)

The reason for the low least-squares efficiencies is high leverage.

```{r, fig.height = 3.4}
h <- phonestudy$leverage[, "p100"]
plot(sort(h), type = "l", lwd = 2, las = 1,
     xlab = "participants, ordered by leverage", ylab = "leverage")
abline(h = 101 / 620, lty = 3)          # what even leverage would give
text(1, 101 / 620, "even leverage", adj = c(0, -0.5), cex = 0.8)
c(max_leverage = max(h), even = 101 / 620)
```

In the $p = 100$ design one participant has leverage
`r f3(max(h))` and so very nearly determines their own fitted value, and a
handful of rows dominate the least-squares fit. Many of these features are
mostly missing, and median imputation turns such a feature into a block of
identical values with a few observed values far from it, which is exactly the
pattern that concentrates leverage. Computing $D^*$ before fitting is how to
see this coming.

## The in-sample signal

The design formulas require a value of `rho2_in`, the population version of
the $R^2$ reported in most regression analyses.

There are two approaches. One is to assume a value, or a series of values, and
examine how the results depend on it. The other is to estimate it. If you
estimate `rho2_in`, use the **adjusted** in-sample $R^2$: the raw statistic is
badly upward-biased, especially when $p$ is large relative to $n$. It is also
wise to examine the values in its **confidence interval**, which inverting the
noncentral $F$ supplies from `n`, `p` and the raw $R^2$ alone.

```{r}
d <- ds[ds$p == 100 & ds$scale == "raw", ]
s <- rho2_from_R2(R2 = d$R2_in, n = d$n, p = d$p)
s
```

Here a raw in-sample $R^2$ of `r f3(s$raw)` becomes an adjusted $R^2$ of
`r f3(s$estimate)`, with 95% interval [`r f3(s$lower)`, `r f3(s$upper)`].

### When there are more predictors than observations

With all 1,821 features, $p + 1 > n$: the least-squares fit is exact and the
adjusted $R^2$ is undefined. `rho2_reml()` estimates `rho2_in` instead, by
restricted maximum likelihood (Patterson and Thompson 1971) under the same
assumption on the coefficients from which the ridge penalty is derived: they
are treated as draws with a common variance, so the outcome's variance has a
signal part proportional to $ZZ'$ and a noise part. It is the estimator used
for the share of trait variance explained by genome-wide markers (Yang et al.
2010), where $p$ also far exceeds $n$. `rho2_from_data()` and
`pred_power(X = , y = )` switch to it automatically when $p + 1 \ge n$.

```{r}
full <- ds[ds$p == 1821 & ds$scale == "raw", ]
full[, c("rho2_in", "rho2_lower", "rho2_upper", "rho2_method", "requires_ridge")]
```

For the full PhoneStudy feature set, the REML estimate is `r f3(full$rho2_in)`
with 95% profile-likelihood interval [`r f3(full$rho2_lower)`,
`r f3(full$rho2_upper)`], well above the `r f3(full$requires_ridge)` that ridge
needs. The estimate is only as good as that assumption: it is close to unbiased
when the signal is spread over many directions or concentrated in the largest
ones, and it fails when the signal sits in the directions of smallest
variance. When $p + 1 < n$ the adjusted $R^2$ makes no such assumption and is
preferable.

## Expected accuracy: `pred_power()`

`pred_power()` puts the pieces together. It reports the expected
out-of-sample statistics, the break-even signal the design requires, and,
when an interval for `rho2_in` is available, the expected out-of-sample $R^2$
at both ends of it. The break-even value (`requires`) is the in-sample signal
at which the expected out-of-sample $R^2$ reaches 0. Put another way, it is
how much of the outcome the covariates need to explain in-sample for the
model to predict new observations better, in expectation, than simply
predicting every unit's outcome with the sample mean.

```{r}
a <- pred_power(n = d$n, p = d$p, R2_in = d$R2_in,
                  Dstar = d$Dstar, Dstar_ridge = d$Dstar_ridge)
summary(a)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
tb <- a$table
ols <- tb[tb$estimator == "ols", ]; rdg <- tb[tb$estimator == "ridge", ]
```

Ordinary least squares (OLS) would need `rho2_in` of at least
`r f3(ols$requires)`, above the upper end of the interval for `rho2_in`
(`r f3(s$upper)`). Its expected out-of-sample $R^2$ is negative everywhere in
that interval, from `r f3(ols$R2oos_lower)` to `r f3(ols$R2oos_upper)`.

Ridge regression trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance, and
needs far less signal: `r f3(rdg$requires)`, below the lower end of the
interval (`r f3(s$lower)`). Its expected out-of-sample $R^2$ runs from
`r f3(rdg$R2oos_lower)` to `r f3(rdg$R2oos_upper)` across the interval, so
ridge is expected to beat the sample mean. The break-even concerns the
expected value: a design that only just meets it beats the sample mean in
roughly half of samples.

Without the covariate matrix, the ridge break-even above uses a planning
approximation to the effective number of parameters, $p_{eff}$, which treats
the covariates as uncorrelated. Computed from the design's own eigenvalues and
ridge leverage, as `pred_power(X = ...)` does when given the features, the
ridge break-even is `r f3(d$requires_ridge)` (the `requires_ridge` column);
`breakeven_rho2(X = X, estimator = "ridge")` gives the same value directly.
Correlated and skewed covariates lower $p_{eff}$, so the planning value is
the more conservative of the two.

Note also that `roos`, the expected correlation, is positive for least
squares even though its expected `R2oos` is negative. A correlation is
unchanged if every prediction is stretched away from or shrunk toward the
mean, so $r^2_{oos}$ is roughly the $R^2_{oos}$ the same predictions could
reach if they were rescaled by the right amount. Least-squares predictions on
this design order participants sensibly but spread them far too widely; ridge's
shrinkage largely corrects that. Reporting both statistics shows whether a
disappointing $R^2_{oos}$ reflects predictions that carry no information or
predictions that carry information on the wrong scale.

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
plot(a)
```

## Transforming the covariates

$D^*$ is sensitive to skewness, which is a property of the measurement scale,
not of the participants. The design efficiency can therefore often be raised
by transforming the covariates:

```{r}
sc <- phonestudy$scalings
sc
```

For the $p = 100$ design, `Dstar` rises from `r f3(sc$Dstar[1])` on the raw
scale to `r f3(sc$Dstar[2])` under a log transform and `r f3(sc$Dstar[3])`
under a rank-normal transform, and the largest leverage falls from
`r f3(sc$max_leverage[1])` to `r f3(sc$max_leverage[3])`. Because this
example also has outcome data, we can see that the realized least-squares
leave-one-out $R^2$ (`R2oos_act`) improves too, from `r f3(sc$R2oos_act[1])`
to `r f3(sc$R2oos_act[3])`. `compare_scalings()` runs the same comparison on
your own covariates.

## Using this for planning

Before collecting data you might ask: what in-sample $R^2$ would this design
need in order to predict new observations better than the sample mean? For
ridge, the `Dstar` argument is $D^*(\kappa^*)$.

```{r}
breakeven_rho2(n = 620, p = 100, Dstar = 0.346)                     # least squares
breakeven_rho2(n = 620, p = 100, Dstar = 0.970, estimator = "ridge") # ridge
```

Alternatively, you can solve for $n$, $p$ or the efficiency factor:

```{r}
solve_n(p = 100, rho2_in = 0.134, Dstar = 0.346)                     # n needed
solve_n(p = 100, rho2_in = 0.134, Dstar = 0.970, estimator = "ridge")
solve_p(n = 620, rho2_in = 0.134, Dstar = 0.346)                     # p affordable
solve_dstar(n = 620, p = 100, rho2_in = 0.134)                       # D* required
```

The last answer is `NA`. Given the other three inputs, even a perfectly even
design would not let least squares beat the sample mean: there is too little
in-sample signal for this number of predictors and this sample size.

```{r, fig.height = 3.8}
plot_breakeven(p = c(25, 100, 200), Dstar = 0.346,
               rho2_in = 0.134, mark_n = 620)
```

Read across at an assumed in-sample $R^2$ to get the sample size $n$ required;
read up at a planned sample size $n$ to get the in-sample $R^2$ required.

Because `rho2_in` is assumed, report a range of values:

```{r}
sensitivity(n = c(300, 620, 1200), p = 100,
            rho2_in = c(0.07, 0.13, 0.20),
            Dstar = 0.346, Dstar_ridge = 0.970)
```

## Caveats

- With $p + 1 \ge n$, `rho2_in` can only be estimated under the ridge prior
  (`rho2_reml()`); treat that estimate with the caution described above.
- Without `X`, ridge approximates `p_eff` by its value for uncorrelated
  covariates (the Marchenko-Pastur form). That is exact for uncorrelated
  covariates at any p/n; correlated or heavy-tailed covariates lower `p_eff`,
  so for them the ridge results are conservative. Supply `X` when you have it.
- Ridge results assume an isotropic prior on the coefficients. In simulation,
  a sparse coefficient vector costs the ridge formulas nothing measurable, but
  collinear covariates make them optimistic.
- The target is leave-one-out cross-validation, and covariates are assumed to
  be measured without error.

## References

Patterson, H. D., and Thompson, R. (1971). Recovery of inter-block information
when block sizes are unequal. *Biometrika*, 58(3), 545–554.

Pargent, F., Schoedel, R., and Stachl, C. (2023). Best practices in supervised
machine learning: A tutorial for psychologists. *Advances in Methods and
Practices in Psychological Science*, 6(3).

Stachl, C., Au, Q., Schoedel, R., Bühner, M., et al. (2020). Predicting
personality from patterns of behavior collected with smartphones.
*Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 117(30), 17680–17687.

Yang, J., Benyamin, B., McEvoy, B. P., et al. (2010). Common SNPs explain a
large proportion of the heritability for human height. *Nature Genetics*,
42(7), 565–569.
